newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Bosnia official criticises reconstruction effort.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia official criticises reconstruction effort.

text.p: A high-level Bosnian official on Wednesday criticised the international community for not providing sufficient aid to the country's shattered industry, hampering reconstruction efforts since 43 months of war ended.

"We're only getting financial support for small enterprises which cannot employ nearly as many people as we have jobless," Dragoljub Stojanov, minister without portfolio in the central Bosnian government, told Reuters during a U.N.-sponsored conference on Bosnia's reconstruction efforts.
"We need to get more international credits to restart production at larger enterprises."

The Bosnian war has cut the country's output to 10 percent of its pre-1991 level and flattened much of its industry, once among the more efficient in the former East bloc. Most of the country's population is out of work, while many Bosnians still rely on food aid for survival.

The international community has pledged $5.1 billion in funds over the next four years to aid the rebuilding of Bosnia's battered infrastructure and industry, seen as a key condition for establishing a lasting peace in the region.
Reconstruction efforts are overseen by the World Bank, while the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has taken on a key role in helping Bosnia to rebuild its financial institutions.

Stojanov said the IMF and the World Bank were to blame in large part for the lack of investment in big enterprises, most of which are in state hands. "They don't believe that these enterprises can work efficiently," he said.

Donors and Bosnians officials over the past few months have signalled they are satisfied with the pace at which aid money is disbursed, but disagreements over how to best use the available funds remain.

Stojanov said there was no point in supporting only small-scale enterprises since that strategy would neither create enough jobs nor generate sufficient exports to provide desperately needed foreign exchange.
"We don't know what to do with all that (donor) money if the World Bank tells us to destroy our big enterprises," he said.
It would only take relatively small capital injections to restart production at a number of companies, mostly in the energy and heavy industry sector, he said.
To supervise properly the restart of production, Stojanov suggested such firms should be placed under the control of international management boards.
Stojanov said the international community should step up efforts to support a decision-making infrastructure to cover both the Moslem-Croat federation and the Bosnian Serb republic.
"Bosnia has become some kind of economic Frankenstein monster because it does not have any instruments of macroeconomic policy at its disposal," Stojanov said.
"If we don't solve these problems soon, we're going to face huge misery among the population and you know what that can mean politically," he added.
